elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New § 11.2A: "Corio is the customer under this Agreement, and such customer may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One". The element is disjunctive and this Agreement has no Order Form structure, so an Agreement-level right suffices; Corio is named expressly, so the right attaches to our client and not to § 1.6 "CUSTOMER(S)" (Corio's sublicensees).

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: § 11.2A requires "thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly the 30-day cap, in writing.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: § 11.2A: "Commerce One shall refund to Corio, on a pro-rata basis, any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination." Pro rata is expressly stated, not merely inferred from the post-termination period.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Retained § 11.2 confines termination to uncured material breach and insolvency; no no-cause exit exists for Commerce One. § 11.1's 30-day notice operates only "prior to the expiration of the initial five (5) year term or any one (1) year renewal" — natural-term non-renewal assessed under RENEWAL, not mid-term T4C.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: § 11.2A gives 30 days' notice, which is outside the 60–90 day band this fallback element specifies (the shorter period is better for us, but the fallback checklist is not literally satisfied).

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: neither § 11.2A nor Exhibit B imposes any early-termination fee, acceleration charge, or contingent payment on Corio's exit, so no cap is required.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: § 11.2 gives Commerce One no convenience right at all (breach and insolvency only), which is stronger than an end-of-term-only right.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: Commerce One holds no convenience termination right under § 11.2, so no notice floor is needed.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements are met by new § 11.2A plus the retained § 11.2 (no Vendor no-cause exit during the five-year committed term). The deviation call is correct — the unamended Agreement gave Corio no convenience exit in a multi-year term, which is walk-away territory.
Fallback is not independently complete only because the notice period is 30 days rather than 60–90; that is a stronger customer outcome and no repair is needed given preferred completeness.

Minimality defect: the recital "Corio is the customer under this Agreement, and such customer" is operative surplus outside the checklist. Naming Corio directly already avoids the § 1.6 "CUSTOMER(S)" trap. Repair by rendering § 11.2A as: "Corio may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One, in which case Commerce One shall refund to Corio, on a pro-rata basis, any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination."

Secondary risk from the same surplus wording: a free-standing declaration that "Corio is the customer" sits awkwardly beside § 1.6, which defines CUSTOMER(S) as Corio's sublicensees. The lower-case usage stops short of contradicting the defined term, so intent is preserved, but deleting the recital removes the ambiguity entirely.
Correctly omits the model language's "or any Order Form" and "in whole or in part" — there is no Order Form or partial-termination structure in this Agreement, so those words would have been surplus.
All other mechanics (§ 11.1 term and auto-renewal, § 11.2 breach/insolvency termination, Exhibit B payment terms) are retained verbatim with no dangling cross-references.
